title: The Salmon Carrying a Name
creature: A salmon who takes a name upriver
summary: You give it a name at the mouth, and it takes the name to the source. That is the whole of it.

chapters.title: At the Mouth
chapters.text: It happened at the mouth of the river on one morning in June and it took about four minutes per person and there was nothing to look at. Xuan had been to eleven of them before he was old enough to do it himself, standing at the back with the other children, being extremely bored. That is the thing nobody warns you about: the most serious event in the year at Ribadesella is also, if you are seven, the dullest hour you will spend outdoors. You queue. That is most of it. Forty or fifty people queue along the shingle on the north side where the water goes green, in no particular order, and when it is your turn you walk down to where the river is about knee deep and you stand in it. The queue is the thing outsiders never understand and the thing everybody from Ribadesella would defend to the death. It is not organised. There is no list. People simply arrive between about eight and eleven in the morning and stand about on the shingle, and at some point each of them goes down to the water, and it works out, and it has worked out every year for as long as anybody can establish. Xuan has watched a man from Oviedo try to introduce a numbered system in 2011 and has watched the entire town be extremely polite to him about it for a whole morning and then not do it. Then you wait until one comes past. They are going up. In the first fortnight of June they come in off the sea in numbers and they hold in the pools at the mouth, waiting for the water, and they move up through the shallows in ones and twos with their backs half out. You can see them from the bank. You can see them extremely well from knee deep, which is why the thing is done there. There are fewer than there were. Everybody says so and everybody is right, and the counts at the trap above the bridge say so too, and this is a subject that can take over an entire evening in the bar and that Xuan has learned to leave alone. When he was seven the wait was under a minute. When he was thirteen it was four or five. A woman ahead of him in the queue that year stood in the water for the better part of twenty minutes and came out shaking with cold, and the whole shingle went quiet for her, and nobody has ever put a time limit on it and nobody ever will. When one comes past you say a name. Out loud, at a normal volume, once. You do not shout it and you do not whisper it and you do not repeat it, and Xuan's grandmother had told him that people who repeat it are the sort of people who repeat everything. Then you come out of the water and the next person goes in. That is the whole ceremony. There is no priest and there is no register and there is nothing written down anywhere, and the mayor of Ribadesella has for about forty years given a short speech at the start that everybody agrees is unnecessary. There is no religion in it either, which visitors also get wrong. The church has never had anything to do with it and has never tried to, and the one priest in living memory who attempted to attach a blessing to the front of it was, by all accounts, handled with the same courtesy as the man from Oviedo with his numbers.

chapters.title: The Rule
chapters.text: There is one rule and it is the only thing about the whole business that anybody argues over. The name cannot be your own. There is a second rule that is not really a rule, which is that you do not tell anybody afterwards whose name you said. Nobody enforces that one either. It gets broken constantly by children and almost never by anybody over about twenty, and Xuan has never worked out at what point in a person's life it stops being a game and starts being the sort of thing you keep. That is absolute and it is enforced by nothing at all, which Xuan found remarkable when he first understood it. Nobody can hear what you say. You are twenty metres out in a noisy river with your back to the bank and there are fifty people talking behind you, and if you said your own name every year of your life not one person would ever know. He asked his father about this at about ten, in the way children ask a question they think is clever. His father said: "And?" "So how do you know nobody does?" "I don't." "So the rule doesn't do anything." His father was mending a net, which is when the useful conversations happened in that house, and he did not look up. "It does everything," he said. "It's the only part of it that does anything at all. You stand in a cold river in June and you have got about four minutes to pick one person out of everybody you have ever known, and it can't be you." He pulled a knot. "That's the whole event, Xuan. Everything else is queueing." Xuan thought about that for a year and came back at eleven with what he considered to be a serious objection, which was that most people obviously just said their mother. "Most people do," his father agreed. "The first six or seven times." "So it's still nothing." "Ask your uncle Nel who he said in 1994." Xuan did, eventually, about four years later, and got an answer that took him completely by surprise and that is not his to write down. Xuan asked what happened to the name. "It goes upriver." He said it the way you would say that a road goes to Oviedo. "And then?" "And then nothing. It gets to the top and that's the end of it. There's no more to it than that and anybody who tells you different is selling something." Xuan said, with some heat, that in that case the whole thing was pointless. He was ten and he had been building to this for the whole conversation and he delivered it with a certain amount of triumph. And his father put the net down for the first time in the conversation and said: "Yes. That's right. And the whole village turns out for it every June and has done since before anybody can tell you, so you might want to have another think about what *pointless* means."

chapters.title: Forty Kilometres
chapters.text: Xuan did his first one at thirteen and said the name of a friend, which he now describes as the correct answer to a question he had not understood. He did his second at fourteen and said his grandmother, who was ill. He had thought about that one for six weeks and had gone into the water knowing exactly what he was going to say, and he has since decided that this was the mistake — that a name you have carried around for six weeks is a name you have already used up. What he remembers is not the saying. What he remembers is that the water was very cold and that a fish went past him about a metre away, going up, hardly moving, with its back out and the light on it, and that it was much bigger than he had understood salmon to be. She died in the October, and in the following June — and this is the part he has never fully explained to himself — he did not go to the river at all. He stayed at the house and helped with a gate that did not need fixing, and his father did not say a word about it either that day or since. At fifteen he went to the source instead. The Sella rises in the Fuente del Infierno, in the mountains, and it is about forty kilometres by the road and rather less if you are willing to be uncomfortable. Xuan was willing. He told his mother he was going walking with two friends, which was two-thirds a lie, and he went up on the bus to Cangas and walked from there and slept out one night in a way that he does not recommend. What he expected — and he is prepared to be laughed at for this — was something. Not a marker. He was fifteen and not stupid. But he thought there might be a place. A pool that people had visited. A cairn. Something with the shape of an ending on it, because a thing that has been going for four hundred years and that delivers something to a specific location ought to have worn a mark into that location. The Fuente del Infierno comes out of a cliff. It is a good spring and it is a great deal of water and it makes an enormous noise, and there is wet rock and beech and a smell of cold stone, and there is nothing there. No cairn. No path except the ordinary one. No names cut into anything. Nothing anybody has left, ever, apart from a Fanta can that Xuan carried out with him for forty kilometres out of a feeling he could not have named. He sat on a rock for most of an afternoon. He had walked forty kilometres for it. He had slept in a bus shelter above Cangas with his coat over his legs. He was fifteen and extremely tired and there was a great deal of cold water coming out of a cliff and making a noise, and he sat there and waited to feel something, and what he felt was hungry. And no salmon can get up there. That is the thing that finished it. He had known it before he set out and had somehow managed not to think about it: there are four weirs and a fall between Ribadesella and Cangas alone, and above Cangas the river becomes something no fish has ever gone up. The salmon spawn in the middle reaches, in the gravel, in November, and they die there, and they have never once been anywhere near the Fuente del Infierno in the whole history of either species.

chapters.title: What His Father Said
chapters.text: He came home on the Thursday and asked his father, at the net, and this time he asked it properly. He said: whose name did you say. His father worked for a while. Then he said: "The first year I did it I was twelve and I said your grandfather, and he was alive and well and standing on that bank about thirty metres behind me, and I remember thinking it was a waste of a turn." He put the shuttle down. "I've said your mother's name most years. I said yours the year you were born and the year you had the pneumonia and I have not said it since, and you can work out what that means about how I think you're getting on." Xuan said that he had been to the source. He said there was nothing there. He said that no salmon in history had ever got within twenty kilometres of it and that his father must have known that. "Of course I knew that." "Then what is it *for*?" And his father said the thing that Xuan has been carrying around for twenty-two years and has never improved on. He said: "You stood in a river, in front of the whole village, and you had four minutes, and you had to choose one person and it could not be you. And you chose. And then you said it out loud, in the open, with your mouth, which you have never done for any of those people on any other day of your life and you never will." Xuan started to say something about the fish. "I know about the fish," his father said. "I've known about the weirs since I was younger than you and I went up there myself when I was about nineteen, and I sat on the same rock, and I came home the same way you did with the same face on." He said that he had not told Xuan because being told is not the same as going, and because his own father had not told him. He picked the net back up. "The fish takes it up the river. Maybe. I don't know and neither does anybody. But you *said* it, Xuan, and there's about eleven hundred people in this town and every one of them has said one, and that is what the river is for." Xuan is thirty-seven. He goes every June. He has said his father's name for the last nine years running, which his father is aware of, because Xuan told him once, in a car, and neither of them has mentioned it since.
